title: Providence cares first for rational beings
source_text: Διὰ πολλῶν δ᾿ ἑξῆς ἐγκαλεῖ ἡμῖν ὡς τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ φάσκουσι πάντα πεποιηκέναι τὸν θεόν. (καὶ) βούλεται ἐκ τῆς περὶ τῶν ζῴων ἱστορίας καὶ τῆς ἐμφαινομένης αὐτοῖς ἀγχινοίας δεικνύναι ὅτι οὐδὲν μᾶλλον ἀνθρώπων ἢ τῶν ἀλόγων ζῴων ἕνεκεν γέγονε τὰ πάντα. καὶ δοκεῖ μοι ὅμοιόν τι εἰπεῖν τοῖς διὰ τὸ πρὸς τοὺς μισουμένους ἔχθος κατηγοροῦσιν αὐτῶν ἐφ᾿ οἷς οἱ φίλτατοι αὐτῶν ἐπαινοῦνται. ὥσπερ γὰρ ἐπὶ τούτων τυφλοῖ τὸ ἔχθος πρὸς τὸ μὴ συνορᾶν ὅτι καὶ φιλτάτων κατηγοροῦσιν δι᾿ ὧν κακῶς λέγειν νομίζουσι τοὺς ἐχθροὺς. τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον καὶ ὁ Κέλσος συγχυθεὶς τὸν λογισμὸν οὐχ ἑώρακεν ὅτι καὶ τῶν ἀπὸ τῆς Στοᾶς φιλοσόφων κατηγορεῖ. οὐ κακῶς προταττόντων τὸν ἄνθρωπον καὶ ἁπαξαπλῶς τὴν λογικὴν φύσιν πάντων τῶν ἀλόγων καὶ διὰ ταύτην λεγόντων προηγουμένως τὴν πρόνοιαν πάντα πεποιηκέναι. καὶ λόγον μὲν ἔχει τὰ λογικὰ, ἅπερ ἐστὶ προηγούμενα. παίδων γεννωμένων· τὰ δ᾿ ἄλογα καὶ τὰ ἄψυχα χορίου συγκτιζομένου τῷ παιδίῳ. καὶ ἡγοῦμαί γε ὅτι, ὥσπερ ἐν ταῖς πόλεσιν οἱ προνοούμενοι τῶν ὠνίων καὶ τῆς ἀγορᾶς δι᾿ οὐδὲν ἄλλο προνοοῦνται ἢ διὰ τοὺς ἀνθρώπους, παραπολαύουσι δὲ τῆς δαψιλείας καὶ κύνες καὶ ἄλλα τῶν ἀλόγων· οὕτως ἡ πρόνοια τῶν μὲν λογικῶν προηγουμένως προνοεῖ, ἐπηκολούθησε δὲ τὸ καὶ τὰ [ἄλλα] ἄλογα ἀπολαύειν τῶν δι᾿ ἀνθρώπους γινομένων. καὶ ὥσπερ ἁμαρτάνει ὁ λέγων τοὺς ἀγορανόμους προνοεῖν οὐ μᾶλλον τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἢ τῶν κυνῶν, ἐπεὶ καὶ οἱ κύνες παραπολαύουσι τῆς δαψιλείας τῶν ὠνίων, οὕτω πολλῷ μᾶλλον Κέλσος καὶ οἱ τὰ αὐτὰ φρονοῦντες αὐτῷ ἀσεβοῦσιν εἰς τὸν προνοοῦντα τῶν λογικῶν θεὸν. φάσκοντες· τί μᾶλλον ἀνθρώποις γίνεσθαι ταῦτα πρὸς τροφὴν ἢ τοῖς φυτοῖς δένδροις τε καὶ πόαις καὶ ἀκάνθαις;
pass_a_gloss: Through many (words) in succession (ἑξῆς) he accuses (ἐγκαλέω) us as saying that God made (ποιέω) all things for man (ἄνθρωπος). And he wishes, from the inquiry (ἱστορία) about animals (ζῷα) and the sagacity (ἀγχίνοια) appearing (ἐμφαίνομαι) in them, to show that not more for the sake of men than of irrational animals (ἄλογα ζῷα) have all things come to be. And he seems to me to say something like those who, through enmity (ἔχθος) toward those hated, accuse (κατηγορέω) them on grounds for which their dearest (φίλτατοι) are praised (ἐπαινέω). For as in their case enmity blinds (τυφλόω) so as not to see together (συνοράω) that they accuse even the dearest through the things by which they think to speak ill (κακῶς λέγω) of the enemies, in the same way Celsus too, confounded (συγχέω) in reasoning (λογισμός), has not seen that he accuses also the philosophers from the Stoa (Στοά), who not badly place first (προτάσσω) man and, in short (ἁπαξαπλῶς), the rational nature (λογικὴ φύσις) before all irrational things, and say that for its sake principally (προηγουμένως) providence (πρόνοια) has made all things. And the rational things, which are principal (προηγούμενα), have the account (λόγον ἔχει) of children being born (γεννάω); the irrational and the soulless (ἄψυχα) of the chorion (χορίον, afterbirth) created together (συγκτίζω) with the infant. — And I think that, as in cities those taking care (προνοέω) of the wares (ὤνια) and the market (ἀγορά) take care for no other reason than for men, but dogs and others of the irrational enjoy besides (παραπολαύω) the abundance (δαψίλεια); so providence takes care principally of the rational, and it followed (ἐπακολουθέω) that the irrational also enjoy (ἀπολαύω) the things coming to be for men. And as he errs (ἁμαρτάνω) who says the market-officers (ἀγορανόμοι) take care not more of men than of dogs, since the dogs too enjoy besides the abundance of wares, so much more Celsus and those thinking the same as he are impious (ἀσεβέω) toward the God who takes care of the rational, saying: Why rather for men do these come to be for food (τροφή) than for plants (φυτά), trees (δένδρα) and grasses (πόαι) and thorns (ἄκανθαι)?
pass_b_english: Next, at great length, he charges us with saying that God made all things for man. And he wants to show, from the natural history of animals and the shrewdness that shows itself in them, that all things have come into being no more for the sake of human beings than for the sake of the irrational animals. He seems to me to say something like those who, out of enmity toward those they hate, accuse them of the very things for which their own dearest friends are praised. For just as with these, hatred blinds them so that they do not see that they are accusing even their dearest friends by the very things through which they think they are speaking ill of their enemies, so in the same way Celsus too, his reasoning thrown into confusion, has not seen that he is also accusing the philosophers of the Stoa. They rightly set man, and in a word the rational nature, above all irrational things, and they say that providence made all things primarily for its sake. And the rational beings, which come first, stand in the place of children being born, while the irrational and the lifeless stand in the place of the afterbirth that is formed along with the child.

And I think that, just as in cities those who look after the goods for sale and the market look after them for no other reason than for the sake of human beings, yet dogs too and others of the irrational animals have a share in the plenty, so providence takes thought primarily for rational beings, and it has followed that the irrational animals also enjoy what is made for human beings. And just as a man is wrong who says that the market officers look after human beings no more than dogs, since the dogs too share in the plenty of the goods for sale, so much more do Celsus and those who think as he does commit impiety against God, who takes thought for rational beings, when they say: “Why are these things produced as food for human beings rather than for plants, for trees and grasses and thorns?”

choices.choice: ‘out of enmity toward those they hate’ (removed redundant ‘hatred for the people they hate’)
διὰ τοὺς ἀνθρώπους: ‘for the sake of human beings’

Celsus’s words: “Why are these things produced … thorns?” His earlier argument (animal history, sagacity) is reported indirectly by Origen and kept so. The sentence about children and afterbirth (λόγον ἔχει … χορίου) is Origen’s statement of the Stoic view; λόγον ἔχει rendered ‘stand in the place of’. διὰ πολλῶν δ᾿ ἑξῆς (‘next, through many words’) rendered ‘Next, at great length’. The bracketed [ἄλλα] before ἄλογα (editorial deletion) is not translated. Possible Scripture background (Genesis 1:26–28) is not explicit and not cited.
